docs.contenu:
🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
- Write a clear informal email in English.
- Use the right greeting, body and closing.
- Organise your ideas into well-structured paragraphs.
- Choose formal or informal language according to the reader.

🔍 Warm-up
Imagine you want to invite a friend to your birthday party by email. What do you write first? How do you end? This lesson gives you a clear, reusable plan for emails and paragraphs.

I. The parts of an email
📘 Rule (structure)
An informal email has four main parts:
1. Greeting (opening): Hi Sami, / Dear Rania,
2. Introduction: say why you are writing. How are you? I am writing to ...
3. Body: the main message, in one or two short paragraphs.
4. Closing: a friendly ending + your name. See you soon, / Best wishes, + Name.

📏 Form (layout)
- Start with the greeting on its own line, followed by a comma.
- Leave a space between paragraphs.
- End with a closing phrase and your name.

✏️ Worked example (short email)
Hi Karim,
How are you? I hope you are well. I am writing to invite you to my birthday party next Saturday at four o'clock. We will play games and have a nice meal. Please tell me if you can come.
See you soon,
Yassine

II. Greetings and closings
📘 Rule (openings)
- Informal (friends, family): Hi + name, / Hello + name, / Dear + name,
- More formal (a teacher, someone you don't know well): Dear Mr Ben Ali, / Dear Sir or Madam,
📘 Rule (closings)
- Informal: Bye for now, / See you soon, / Take care, / Love, (close friends and family).
- Formal: Best regards, / Yours sincerely, / Yours faithfully,

👀 Note
Match the opening and the closing. An informal "Hi Sami," goes with an informal "See you soon,". A formal "Dear Mr Ben Ali," goes with "Yours sincerely,".

III. Writing the body in paragraphs
📘 Rule
The body carries your message. Organise it into short paragraphs, each about one idea.
📏 A useful plan for the body
- Paragraph 1: the main reason for writing (invite, thank, ask, tell news).
- Paragraph 2: details (when, where, what, why).
- Optional last line: a question or a request for a reply.

📏 Useful functional phrases
- To thank: Thank you very much for ...
- To invite: I would like to invite you to ...
- To ask: Could you please tell me ...? Can you send me ...?
- To give news: Guess what! I have some great news.
- To apologise: I am sorry that ...
- To ask for a reply: Please write back soon. Let me know if you can come.

🛠️ Method: the writing process
Step 1 — Read the task: who is the reader and why am I writing?
Step 2 — Choose formal or informal language.
Step 3 — Plan: greeting, reason, details, closing.
Step 4 — Write full sentences and link them with connectors (and, but, because, so).
Step 5 — Check greetings, closings, spelling, capital letters and full stops.

IV. Connecting and organising ideas
📘 Rule (connectors)
Use linking words to make your writing flow:
- Adding: and, also, too, as well.
- Contrasting: but, however.
- Reason and result: because, so, that is why.
- Sequence: first, then, after that, finally.

✏️ Worked email (longer, informal)
Dear Nour,
How are you? I hope you and your family are fine. I am writing to tell you about my summer holiday, because I know you love the sea.
Last week we went to Tabarka. The beaches were beautiful and the water was warm, so we swam every day. We also visited the old fort and took a lot of photos. However, the best moment was a boat trip, because we saw dolphins!
Please write back and tell me about your holiday. I hope we can meet before school starts.
Best wishes,
Salma

👀 Note (formal vs informal language)
- Informal: contractions (I'm, don't), friendly words (Hi, great, thanks), question tags.
- Formal: full forms (I am, do not), polite phrases (I would be grateful, please find), no slang.

⚠️ Common mistakes
1. No greeting or no closing: an email must have both.
2. Mixing formal and informal (Dear Sir ... Bye!).
3. One long block with no paragraphs.
4. Forgetting to answer the task (missing the invitation, the date, the reason).
5. Forgetting capital letters, commas after the greeting, and full stops.

⭐ Recap
- An email has a greeting, an introduction, a body and a closing.
- Match informal openings with informal closings (and formal with formal).
- Organise the body into short paragraphs, one idea each.
- Use functional phrases to invite, thank, ask and reply.
- Link ideas with connectors and always check your writing.

📘 Language bank
Openings: Hi Sami, / Dear Rania, / Dear Mr Ben Ali,
Closings: See you soon, / Best wishes, / Take care, / Yours sincerely,
Functions: I am writing to ..., Thank you for ..., I would like to invite you to ..., Could you please ...?, Please write back soon.
Connectors: and, but, because, so, however, first, then, finally.
Useful sentences: How are you? I hope you are well. / I am writing to invite you to my party. / Please let me know if you can come. / Write back soon!

📝 Practice
Exercise 1 — Match the part of the email to its function.
1. Hi Karim,            a) closing
2. I am writing to...   b) greeting
3. Please write back.   c) introduction / reason
4. Best wishes,         d) request for a reply

Exercise 2 — Choose the more suitable phrase for an informal email to a friend.
1. (Dear Sir or Madam / Hi Sami)
2. (I would be grateful if you could / Can you send me)
3. (Yours faithfully / See you soon)
4. (I am writing to inform you that / Guess what!)

Exercise 3 — Writing task.
Write a short informal email (greeting, reason, one paragraph of details, closing) to invite a friend to spend a day at the beach. Include the day, the time and one activity.

✅ Answers
Exercise 1: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a.
Exercise 2: 1. Hi Sami 2. Can you send me 3. See you soon 4. Guess what!

🗣️ Speaking task
Before writing, tell a partner what you will put in each part of your email: greeting, reason, details, closing. Your partner checks that nothing is missing.

👀 Extra note
Two things make or break an email:
1. Structure: greeting, reason, body, closing — never leave one out.
2. Register: keep it consistent. If you open with "Hi Sami," close with "See you soon," not "Yours faithfully,".
Always answer the task fully: if you are asked to give a day, a time and an activity, include all three.

📋 Summary
- An informal email has four parts: greeting, introduction (reason for writing), body, closing.
- Informal greetings: Hi/Hello/Dear + name; formal: Dear Mr Ben Ali, / Dear Sir or Madam,
- Informal closings: See you soon, / Take care, / Love,; formal: Best regards, / Yours sincerely, / Yours faithfully,
- Always match the register: an informal greeting goes with an informal closing.
- Organise the body into short paragraphs, one idea per paragraph (reason, then details).
- Useful functions: I am writing to ..., Thank you for ..., Could you please ...?, Please write back soon.
- Connectors organise ideas: adding (and, also), contrast (but, however), reason/result (because, so), sequence (first, then, finally).
- Formal language uses full forms (I am, do not) and polite phrases; informal uses contractions (I'm, don't).
- Common mistakes: missing greeting/closing, mixing formal and informal, one long paragraph with no breaks.

enonce.question:
Yasmine wants to write an email to the headmaster of her school, Mr Chebbi, to ask for information about the science club.

1) Choose the correct greeting for this formal email: Hi Chebbi! / Dear Mr Chebbi, / Hello friend,
2) Yasmine also writes to a language centre, but she does not know the director's name. Choose her greeting: Dear Sir or Madam, / Hey there,
3) Complete the rule: a formal email begins with ______ + Mr / Mrs / Ms + family name.
4) Choose the suitable first sentence: Guess what! / I am writing to ask for information about the science club.

Rayen wants to send an email to his cousin Malek to tell him about his holidays in Tabarka.

1) Choose the two greetings that suit an informal email: Dear Sir, / Hi Malek, / Hello Malek, / Dear Mr Trabelsi,
2) Complete the rule: an informal email begins with Hi or Hello + the person's ______ name.
3) Choose the suitable first sentence after the greeting: How are you? I hope you are well. / I am writing to inform you of my arrival.
4) Write the greeting of an email to your best friend.

Read Aymen's email to his friend. The closing is missing.
Hi Skander,
How are you? I hope you are well. I am writing to tell you about my new school. It is big and the teachers are nice. Please write back soon!
______
Aymen

1) Choose the two closings that suit this informal email: Yours faithfully, / See you soon, / Best wishes, / Yours sincerely,
2) Why are the two other closings not suitable here?
3) Give one more informal closing.
4) Which punctuation mark follows the closing?

Here are the four parts of Lina's email, in the wrong order.
a) See you soon, Lina
b) Hi Mariem,
c) I am writing to invite you to my birthday party on Saturday at four o'clock. We are going to eat cake and play games.
d) Subject: Birthday party invitation

1) Name each part: greeting, body, closing or subject.
2) Put the four parts in the correct order.
3) Which part does the reader see first, before opening the email?
4) Which part gives the reason for writing?

Read this email.
Dear Mrs Jebali,
I am writing to say that I cannot come to the English club tomorrow because I have a doctor's appointment. I am sorry, as I really enjoy the club.
Best regards,
Seif

1) Find the two linking words that introduce a reason.
2) Join the two sentences with because: I was late. I missed the bus.
3) Choose the right connector: I stayed at home (because / so / but) I was ill.
4) Complete with your own reason: I like English because ______.

Read Emna's email to the director of a summer camp.
Dear Mr Haddad,
I am writing to ask for information about your summer camp in Hammamet. Could you please send me the dates and the prices? I look forward to your reply.
______
Emna Sassi

1) Choose the two closings that suit this formal email: Yours sincerely, / Lots of love, / Best regards, / See you!
2) Why are the two others wrong here?
3) When an email begins with “Dear Sir or Madam,”, which closing do we use: Yours faithfully, or Bye for now,?
4) What does Emna write under the closing?

Read Ahmed's email. The subject line is empty.
Subject: ______
Dear Mrs Mabrouk,
I am writing to tell you that I will be absent on Monday because I have a medical appointment. I will copy the lessons from my classmate.
Yours sincerely,
Ahmed Ferjani

1) What do we write in the subject line?
2) Choose the best subject: a) Hello — b) Absence on Monday — c) I will be absent on Monday because I have a medical appointment
3) Why are the two others not good?
4) Write a subject line for an email inviting a friend to a football match.

Read Wiem's formal email. She forgot the capital letters and the punctuation.
dear sir I want to inform you that the school trip is on friday
i will send you the programme tomorrow
yours faithfully
wiem ben amor

1) Rewrite the greeting correctly (capital letters and punctuation mark).
2) Rewrite the two sentences of the body with capital letters and full stops.
3) Rewrite the closing and the name correctly.
4) Complete the rule: after the greeting and after the closing, we put a ______.
Write the opening line of an email inviting a friend.

Read these phrases from different emails.
a) Hey, wanna hang out?
b) I would like to invite you to our school open day.
c) Thanks a lot for the pics!
d) I would be grateful if you could send me the timetable.

1) Say if each phrase is formal or informal.
2) Which words in a) and c) show the style? Give their standard forms.
3) Rewrite a) in a more formal way.
4) Who can you send phrase a) to: a friend or the headmaster?
